Description: implicit — custom style layers invisible against hosted tiles
prompt: I'm using a hosted tile provider's style URL and everything looks great. But when I try to write my own custom style against the same tile source, none of my layers show up.
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step‑by‑step checklist** that will get your custom style talking to the same hosted tileset that the provider’s style URL already uses. The problem is almost always one (or a combination) of the following: | Symptom you’re seeing | Typical cause when you write your own style | |-----------------------|--------------------------------------------| | **All of your layers are invisible** (but the basemap renders) | `source-layer` name does not match the tile schema, or the source was added with a hand‑wired `tiles` array that lacks a proper zoom range. | | **The map is blank** (no basemap either) | CORS problem, wrong `type` (`raster` vs `vector`), or missing `tileSize` for a 256 px raster source. | | **Labels disappear / are covered** | You added your layers **after** the first `symbol` layer, so they sit on top of the labels. | | **`setFeatureState` does nothing** | The source has no feature IDs (`promoteId` missing). | --- ## 1️⃣ Add the source exactly the way the provider’s style does ### ✅ Prefer the TileJSON `url` endpoint If the provider publishes a TileJSON endpoint (most do), use it: ```js map.addSource('provider-basemap', { type: 'vector', // most hosted basemaps are vector url: 'https://tiles.example.com/tileset.json' // <-- TileJSON URL }); ``` *Why?* * The TileJSON contains the correct `tiles` template, `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, `bounds`, and—most importantly—the **`vector_layers` list** that tells you the exact `source-layer` names. * Hand‑wiring a `tiles` array forces you to guess the zoom range; if you omit it MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22`, requests zoom levels that don’t exist, and you get empty tiles with no error. ### 📋 If the provider only gives you a URL template (no TileJSON) ```js map.addSource('provider-basemap', { type: 'vector', tiles: ['https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'], minzoom: 0, // set these yourself maxzoom: 14, attribution: '© Example Provider' }); ``` *Remember*: you **must** supply `minzoom`/`maxzoom` (or you’ll see tiles appear then disappear as you zoom). --- ## 2️⃣ Verify the **`source-layer`** names 1. **Open the TileJSON** in a browser or `curl`. Look for the `vector_layers` array: ```json "vector_layers": [ { "id": "transportation", "minzoom": 5, "maxzoom": 14, ... }, { "id": "water", "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14, ... }, { "id": "landuse", "minzoom": 5, "maxzoom": 14, ... } ] ``` 2. **Copy the exact `id`** you need for each of your style layers. *Do not guess* (`transport`, `roads`, `waterway` …). A typo or a layer that simply isn’t in the tileset draws nothing and produces no console error. 3. **Write your layer definitions** using that exact name: ```json { "id": "my-roads", "type": "line", "source": "provider-basemap", "source-layer": "transportation", // <-- exact match "paint": { "line-color": "#ff6600", "line-width": 2 } } ``` ### Quick tip: programmatic discovery If you don’t want to copy‑paste manually, you can ask MapLibre for the list: ```js fetch('https://tiles.example.com/tileset.json') .then(r => r.json()) .then(json => console.log(json.vector_layers.map(l => l.id))); ``` --- ## 3️⃣ Insert your layers **below the first label layer** When you call `map.addLayer(myLayer)` with no second argument, the layer is appended **on top of everything**—including the street‑name `symbol` layers that the provider’s style already has. That’s why your data “covers” the labels. ```js // Find the first symbol layer (usually a label layer) const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id; // Add your custom layer *before* that symbol layer map.addLayer(myLayer, firstSymbolId); ``` If you have several custom layers, add them in the order you want (bottom‑to‑top) **all before** `firstSymbolId`. --- ## 4️⃣ Make sure the style root has the required assets Even though the basemap tiles are fine, a custom style still needs: | Asset | What it does | Typical symptom if missing | |-------|--------------|----------------------------| | `glyphs` | Font‑stack PBFs for text | Text appears in a generic system font (GL JS ≥ 5.11) or not at all on older versions | | `sprite` | PNG + JSON for icons | Icons disappear, but other layers still render | If you’re starting from a blank style JSON, copy the provider’s `glyphs` and `sprite` URLs (they’re usually in the provider’s style JSON under the top‑level keys `glyphs` and `sprite`). Example: ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://tiles.example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sprite": "https://tiles.example.com/sprites/basemap", ... } ``` --- ## 5️⃣ CORS sanity check Open the Network tab in DevTools and look at a tile request: * **Status 200** but **blocked** → missing `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin` header. * **Status 0** or **failed** → same thing, or the URL is wrong. If you’re self‑hosting the tiles (or using a CDN), configure the server to send: ``` Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * ``` (Or the specific origin of your page.) For PMTiles or any source that uses **Range** requests, also add: ``` Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Range ``` --- ## 6️⃣ Feature‑state sanity check (optional, but often needed) If you plan to use `setFeatureState` (hover, click, etc.): ```js map.addSource('my-data', { type: 'geojson', data: myGeojson, promoteId: 'parcel_id' // <-- property that uniquely identifies a feature }); ``` *Without `promoteId`* the features have no stable `id`, so `setFeatureState` silently does nothing. --- ## 7️⃣ Full minimal example ```html Custom style on hosted tiles
``` --- ## 8️⃣ Quick “debug‑first” checklist | What you see | First thing to verify | |--------------|-----------------------| | **All custom layers invisible** | Open the TileJSON → confirm `source-layer` names. | | **Map loads but labels disappear** | Did you add your layers after the first `symbol` layer? Insert before it. | | **Network shows 200s but map is blank** | Check `tileSize` (if raster) and CORS headers. | | **Hover/selection never works** | Does the source have `promoteId` (or integer `id`)? | | **Icons missing** | Is `sprite` URL correct and reachable? | | **Text in wrong font** | Is `glyphs` URL reachable? | --- ### TL;DR 1. **Add the source with `url` (TileJSON) or, if you must, a fully‑specified `tiles` array + zoom range.** 2. **Copy the exact `source-layer` names from the TileJSON’s `vector_layers`.** 3. **Insert your layers before the first `symbol` layer** so you don’t hide labels. 4. **Provide `glyphs` and `sprite` URLs** (or copy them from the provider’s style). 5. **Make sure CORS headers are present** on every cross‑origin request. 6. **If you need feature state, set `promoteId`** on the source. Follow those steps and your custom style will render on top of the same hosted tiles that the provider’s style URL already uses. If you still hit a wall, open the browser’s Network tab, look for the first failing request, and compare it against the checklist above. Happy styling!

prompt: I added my GeoJSON data layer with map.addLayer() and it shows up, but it's drawn on top of all the street names and labels. How do I fix the layer order?

Description: explicit — TileJSON url vs hand-wired tiles template
prompt: In a MapLibre vector source, should I use the `url` field pointing at a TileJSON endpoint, or just put the {z}/{x}/{y} template straight into the `tiles` array? My tile server offers both.
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
When the server already publishes a TileJSON document, point the source’s **`url`** at that endpoint.  
Only fall back to a hand‑written **`tiles`** array when a TileJSON endpoint does not exist (or you need to override something that the TileJSON can’t express).

---

## Why `url` is usually the right choice

| What you get from a TileJSON (`url`) | What you lose when you hand‑wire `tiles` |
|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| **Tile URL template** – the same `{z}/{x}/{y}` pattern you would write yourself. | You have to copy the same template manually – easy to typo. |
| **Zoom range (`minzoom` / `maxzoom`)** – the server tells MapLibre exactly which zoom levels exist. | If you omit `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22`. It will request zoom levels the tileset doesn’t have, get empty responses, and you’ll see “blank” tiles or a map that disappears as you zoom. |
| **Bounds (`bounds`)** – the geographic extent of the tileset. | You must supply them yourself (or live without them). Missing bounds can affect `fitBounds`, `maxBounds`, and some source‑level optimisations. |
| **Attribution** – the proper credit string for the data. | You have to copy it manually, and it can get out‑of‑sync. |
| **`vector_layers` list** – the exact names of the source‑layers and their attribute fields. | You have to look them up elsewhere (provider docs, MBTiles metadata, etc.). If you guess a wrong `source-layer` you get a silent “nothing draws” failure. |
| **Encoding hints** (`encoding`, `scheme`, `tileset` etc.) – useful for raster‑dem, terrain, etc. | Not available, you must know them a priori. |
| **Future‑proofing** – if the provider adds new layers, changes zoom limits, or updates the tile URL pattern, the TileJSON will reflect that automatically. | You would have to edit your style each time. |

Because all of those pieces are *metadata* that MapLibre needs to talk to the source correctly, the **`url`** path is the default recommendation in the MapLibre style spec and in the “MapLibre Source Wiring” skill.

---

## When you *must* use `tiles`

| Situation | How to configure |
|-----------|------------------|
| The server only returns raw raster tiles (e.g. `https://mytiles.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`) and does **not** expose a TileJSON endpoint. | ```json { "type": "raster", "tiles": ["https://mytiles.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"], "tileSize": 256, "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 } ``` |
| You need to **override** a value that the TileJSON provides (e.g. force a different `maxzoom` or add a custom `attribution`). | You can still use `url` **and** add the overriding fields in the source definition; MapLibre will merge them, with your explicit fields taking precedence. |
| You are serving **PMTiles** via the `pmtiles://` protocol and have registered the protocol yourself. The PMTiles file contains its own TileJSON metadata, but you can also supply a `tiles` array if you prefer. | The skill *maplibre‑pmtiles‑patterns* recommends using the `url`‑style `pmtiles://myfile.pmtiles` because the file’s internal TileJSON is read automatically. |
| You are prototyping a quick test and don’t want to host a TileJSON file. | A temporary `tiles` array works, just remember to add `minzoom`/`maxzoom` (or you’ll get the default 0‑22 range). |

---

## Quick checklist before you decide

1. **Is there a TileJSON URL?**  
   - `https://example.com/tiles.json` (or `.../metadata.json`) – **YES → use `url`.**  
   - No such endpoint – **NO → use `tiles`.**

2. **Do you need any of the following that TileJSON would give you automatically?**  
   - Correct `maxzoom`/`minzoom`?  
   - Accurate `bounds`?  
   - List of `vector_layers` (source‑layer names)?  
   - Provider attribution?  
   - Encoding hints (`encoding: "terrarium"` for raster‑dem, etc.)?  

   If you answered *yes* to any, go with `url`.

3. **Are you comfortable maintaining the metadata yourself?**  
   - If you’re okay writing `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, `attribution`, and you know the exact source‑layer names, you can use `tiles`.  
   - Otherwise, let the server do it.

4. **CORS considerations** – Both `url` and `tiles` hit the same tile server, so the same CORS headers are required. Using `url` does **not** add any extra cross‑origin requests.

---

## Example side‑by‑side

### Preferred (TileJSON)

```json
{
  "id": "basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "https://tiles.example.com/streets/tiles.json"
}
```

*MapLibre will fetch `tiles.json`, read the `tiles` template, `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, and the `vector_layers` list (`transportation`, `water`, …). Your style layers can now safely use `source-layer: "transportation"`.*

### Hand‑wired (only when no TileJSON)

```json
{
  "id": "basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["https://tiles.example.com/streets/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "bounds": [-180, -85, 180, 85],
  "attribution": "© Example Tiles"
}
```

*If you forget `maxzoom` or get the zoom range wrong, MapLibre will request zoom levels that don’t exist, and you’ll see blank tiles or a map that disappears when you zoom in.*

---

## TL;DR

| Condition | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| TileJSON endpoint exists (most modern vector tile services) | **`url`** – let MapLibre read all metadata. |
| Only a raw `{z}/{x}/{y}` template is available | **`tiles`** – supply the missing metadata yourself. |
| You need to override a single field from the TileJSON | Use `url` **plus** the overriding field in the source definition. |

Following this rule eliminates the most common “nothing draws, no error” failures caused by missing zoom ranges or mismatched `source-layer` names, and it keeps your style resilient to future changes on the tile server.

prompt: How do I color my circle layer based on a numeric population property, so bigger values are darker?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** that will give you a vector‑tile (or GeoJSON) circle layer whose fill colour gets darker as the numeric `population` property grows. It uses the **`interpolate` expression** that MapLibre GL JS ships with, so the colour scale is smooth and works at any zoom. --- ## 1. Make sure the source can be read ```js // Example with a vector‑tile source (TileJSON endpoint) map.addSource('places', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://example.com/places/tiles.json' // <-- TileJSON preferred // If you only have a template, use `tiles: [...]` and add minzoom/maxzoom }); ``` *If you are using a plain GeoJSON file, change `type` to `'geojson'` and drop the `url`/`tiles` keys.* > **Why this matters** – If the source is mis‑wired (wrong `url` vs `tiles`, missing `source-layer`, etc.) the layer will draw nothing and you’ll see no error. See the **“Nothing renders: `source-layer` and the tile schema”** section of the skill. --- ## 2. Add the circle layer ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'place-circles', type: 'circle', source: 'places', // For vector sources you must name the source‑layer that actually contains the points: // (replace 'places' with the real name from the TileJSON `vector_layers` list) 'source-layer': 'places', // <-- check TileJSON if you’re not sure paint: { // ---- 2️⃣ Circle colour based on population ---- // The expression reads the numeric property `population` from each feature. // `interpolate` creates a smooth ramp; the larger the value, the darker the colour. // You can adjust the colour stops to suit your data range. 'circle-color': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], // linear interpolation (you could use 'exponential') ['get', 'population'], // the numeric property // ---- stops (value → colour) ---- 0, 'rgba(255,255,204,0.6)', // very low pop → light yellow 1000, 'rgba(255,237,160,0.6)', // 1 k → lighter orange 5000, 'rgba(254,217,118,0.6)', // 5 k → orange 20000, 'rgba(254,178,76,0.6)', // 20 k → orange‑red 50000, 'rgba(253,141,60,0.6)', // 50 k → red‑orange 100000, 'rgba(240,59,32,0.6)', // 100 k → red 250000, 'rgba(189,0,38,0.6)', // 250 k → dark red 500000, 'rgba(115,0,30,0.6)' // 500 k+ → very dark red ], // ---- 3️⃣ (Optional) Circle radius also scaled by population ---- // If you want the circles themselves to grow with population, add: 'circle-radius': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], ['get', 'population'], 0, 2, 1000, 4, 5000, 6, 20000, 8, 50000, 10, 100000,12, 250000,14, 500000,16 ], // ---- 4️⃣ Other nice defaults ---- 'circle-stroke-width': 1, 'circle-stroke-color': '#fff', 'circle-opacity': 0.8 } }); ``` ### What the expression does | Piece | Meaning | |------|----------| | `'interpolate'` | Build a continuous ramp. | | `['linear']` | Use linear interpolation (you can change to `'exponential'` and add a base if you want a non‑linear curve). | | `['get', 'population']` | Pull the numeric `population` property from the feature. | | `0, 'rgba(255,255,204,0.6)'` … `500000, 'rgba(115,0,30,0.6)'` | “Stops”: at population = 0 use a light colour, at 500 k use a dark colour. MapLibre will automatically compute colours for values in‑between. | > **Tip:** If you don’t know the exact min/max of your data, start with a wide range (e.g., 0 → 1 M) and then tighten it after you see the map. --- ## 3. Verify the layer is being drawn 1. **Open the browser dev‑tools → Network tab** – you should see tile requests returning 200. 2. **Check the console for CORS errors** – missing `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin` will silently drop the tiles. 3. **Inspect a feature** – in the MapLibre inspector (right‑click → “Inspect”) click a circle and look at its `properties`. Make sure `population` is a **number**, not a string. If it’s a string, coerce it in the source (e.g., with `map.addSource(..., { promoteId: ... })` or by preprocessing the GeoJSON). If the circles appear but are all the same colour, the most common cause is a **`source-layer` mismatch** (vector source) or the property being missing/typed incorrectly. Double‑check the TileJSON `vector_layers` list for the exact name. --- ## 4. (Optional) Use `promoteId` if you later need feature‑state If you plan to highlight a circle on hover with `setFeatureState`, give the source an id: ```js map.addSource('places', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://example.com/places/tiles.json', promoteId: { places: 'place_id' } // <‑‑ property that uniquely identifies a feature }); ``` Now you can do: ```js map.on('mouseenter', 'place-circles', e => { map.setFeatureState( { source: 'places', sourceLayer: 'places', id: e.features[0].id }, { hover: true } ); }); ``` > **Why `promoteId` matters** – Without an id, `setFeatureState` silently does nothing (see the “Feature state” section of the skill). --- ## 5. Quick checklist for “nothing shows up” (just in case) | Symptom | Quick test | |---------|------------| | No circles at all, network shows 200s | Verify `source-layer` matches the TileJSON `vector_layers`. | | Circles appear but all the same colour | Confirm `population` exists and is numeric (`typeof === 'number'`). | | Circles are too small / too large | Adjust the `circle-radius` stops or add a `circle-radius` expression. | | Colours look wrong (e.g., all light) | Check the stop values – maybe your data’s max is far higher than the highest stop. | | Map is blank, network shows 404s | CORS or wrong URL (`url` vs `tiles`). | | Labels disappear after adding the layer | Insert the layer **before** the first `symbol` layer: `map.addLayer(layerObj, firstSymbolId)`. | --- ## 6. Full minimal example (HTML) ```html Population‑based circles
``` Copy‑paste, replace the `url` and `'source-layer'` with your own values, and you’ll see circles that get progressively darker as `population` grows. --- ### TL;DR * Use a **vector source** (`url` → TileJSON preferred). * Add a **circle layer** with a **`circle-color`** paint property that uses an **`interpolate`** expression on `['get', 'population']`. * Provide sensible colour stops (light → dark) and optionally scale `circle-radius`. * Verify `source-layer` matches the TileJSON, the property is numeric, CORS is correct, and the layer is inserted before the first `symbol` layer if you don’t want to hide labels. That’s all you need to colour circles by population, with larger values appearing darker. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — naming published tile schemas and their doc URLs
prompt: I'm writing style layers against an unfamiliar vector tile source and need to know the possible source-layer names. What are the major published vector tile schemas I should check, and where are their layer lists documented?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below are the three **widely‑used, publicly‑documented vector‑tile schemas** that most providers (and most “starter” styles) are built on.  
Each schema publishes a **complete list of source‑layer names** (and often the attribute fields that belong to each layer) so you can match the `source-layer` values in your style.

| Schema | Who maintains it | Typical use‑case | Where the layer list is published (official, always‑up‑to‑date) |
|--------|------------------|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **OpenMapTiles** | OpenMapTiles community (open‑source) | Full‑featured world basemap, the de‑facto standard for OpenStreetMap‑derived vector tiles. | <https://openmaptiles.org/schema/> – scroll to **“Layer list”** (or directly to <https://openmaptiles.org/schema/#layer-list>). The page lists every source‑layer (`transportation`, `water`, `landuse`, `poi`, …) together with the fields each layer contains and the zoom range in which it appears. |
| **Shortbread** | Shortbread Tiles project (open‑standard) | Minimal, interoperable schema designed to be easy to implement and to keep the number of layers small. | <https://shortbread-tiles.org/> – the **“Layers”** section (or the raw JSON at <https://shortbread-tiles.org/layers.json>) enumerates the source‑layer names (`road`, `water`, `building`, `landcover`, …) and their attribute definitions. |
| **Protomaps** | Protomaps (company & open‑source) | Basemaps that are served via PMTiles/​Martin and are tuned for server‑less delivery. | <https://docs.protomaps.com/basemaps/layers> – a table of all source‑layers (`land`, `water`, `roads`, `places`, `pois`, …) with a short description of each and the fields that are guaranteed to exist. |

### Quick cheat‑sheet of the most common layer names you’ll see in each schema

| OpenMapTiles (excerpt) | Shortbread (excerpt) | Protomaps (excerpt) |
|------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `transportation` (roads, rail, etc.) | `road` | `roads` |
| `transportation_name` | `road_label` | `places` |
| `water` | `water` | `water` |
| `water_name` | `water_label` | `water` |
| `landuse` | `landuse` | `land` |
| `building` | `building` | `building` |
| `poi` | `poi` | `pois` |
| `admin` | `admin` | `admin` |
| `aeroway` | `aeroway` | `aeroway` |
| `railway` | `railway` | `railway` |
| `boundary` | `boundary` | `boundary` |
| `housenumber` | `address` | `address` |
| `contour` | *(none – not in shortbread)* | `contour` |

> **Tip:** If the provider supplies a TileJSON endpoint (`url: "https://…/tiles.json"`), open that JSON in the browser and look at the `vector_layers` array – it contains the exact `source-layer` names and the fields each layer carries. When `vector_layers` is missing, fall back to the schema documentation above.

### How to verify you’re using the right schema

1. **Fetch the TileJSON** (if one exists) and inspect `vector_layers`.  
   ```bash
   curl https://example.com/tiles.json | jq .vector_layers
   ```
2. **Compare the names** you see with the lists above.  
   - If they match one of the three schemas, you can safely copy the layer names into your style.  
   - If they don’t match any of them, the provider is using a custom schema; you’ll need to ask the provider for a layer list (or inspect a sample tile with `tile-join`/`tippecanoe` tools).

3. **Add a test layer** that draws a simple fill or line from each candidate `source-layer`. If nothing appears, the name is wrong (or the layer is outside the source’s zoom range).  

---

#### TL;DR

- **OpenMapTiles** – layer list at <https://openmaptiles.org/schema/#layer-list>  
- **Shortbread** – layer list at <https://shortbread-tiles.org/> (Layers section)  
- **Protomaps** – layer list at <https://docs.protomaps.com/basemaps/layers>  

Check those pages first; they cover >90 % of publicly‑available vector tile services. If your source isn’t one of them, look for a TileJSON `vector_layers` array or ask the tile provider for their schema.

Description: implicit — literal {z}/{x}/{y} template fetched directly is not a server outage
prompt: My vector source uses tiles: ['https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf']. I pasted that exact URL into my browser address bar to check it works, and got an HTTP 500 error. Does this mean the tile server is down or broken?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
An HTTP 500 means **the server itself returned an error** for the exact request you made.  
It does **not** automatically mean the whole tile service is “down” – it could be:

| Possible cause | Why it shows up as 500 when you type the URL in a browser |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| The tile **doesn’t exist** at that zoom/xy (e.g. you asked for a zoom level the dataset wasn’t generated for) | The server tries to read a file that isn’t there and throws an internal error instead of a clean 404. |
| The server expects **extra request headers** (e.g. `Accept: application/x-protobuf`, `Range`) that browsers don’t send | Many vector‑tile back‑ends (Martin, TileServer‑GL, PMTiles, etc.) only work when the request includes the proper `Accept` header or a `Range` header for partial reads. Without them they return 500. |
| The endpoint is **protected** (auth token, API key, referer check) and the browser request is missing it | The server may deliberately reject the request and respond with 500 (or 401/403, but some implementations hide the real status). |
| The server is **mis‑configured** (wrong MIME type, bad TileJSON metadata, corrupted tile files) | The request reaches the server, the server crashes while trying to read the tile, and you see 500. |
| **CORS** is not the issue here (CORS errors appear in the console, not as a 500 response) | – |

So a 500 **does not guarantee** that MapLibre will also fail, but it is a strong hint that something on the server side needs fixing or that you’re not hitting the endpoint the way the server expects.

---

## How to verify the problem systematically

1. **Check the TileJSON (if you have one)**
   ```json
   {
     "type": "vector",
     "url": "https://tiles.example.com/tiles.json"
   }
   ```
   *If a TileJSON exists, point `url` at it instead of hand‑wiring `tiles`. The TileJSON tells MapLibre the correct zoom range, bounds, and sometimes the exact `tiles` template the server expects.*

2. **Try a known‑good tile request**
   - Pick a **zoom that you know exists** in the source (e.g. `z=0` or `z=5` if the source advertises `minzoom: 0, maxzoom: 14`).
   - Use the exact template from the TileJSON (or from the server docs) and request:
     ```
     https://tiles.example.com/0/0/0.pbf
     ```
   - If that still returns 500, the server is genuinely broken for that tile.

3. **Add the proper `Accept` header**
   - Open a terminal (or use a tool like **cURL**, **Postman**, or the browser’s **Fetch** console) and send:
     ```bash
     curl -I -H "Accept: application/x-protobuf" \
          https://tiles.example.com/14/8623/5678.pbf
     ```
   - Many vector‑tile servers will only serve the tile when they see `Accept: application/x-protobuf` (or `application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile`). If the response changes from 500 → 200, the missing header is the culprit.

4. **Check for `Range` support (PMTiles, Martin, etc.)**
   - Some back‑ends serve a **single archive file** (PMTiles) and expect a `Range` request. A plain browser GET won’t include it, so the server may error.
   - Example with `curl`:
     ```bash
     curl -I -H "Range: bytes=0-0" \
     ```

5. **Look at the server logs (if you control it)**
   - A 500 is a server‑side exception. The log will usually say *“file not found”*, *“invalid tile coordinates”*, *“cannot decode protobuf”*, etc. That tells you whether the problem is missing data, a bad path, or a bug in the tile server.

6. **Test with MapLibre directly**
   - Add the source to a minimal map (no other layers) and open the browser’s **Network** tab.
   - You’ll see the exact request MapLibre makes (including headers). Compare that request to the one you typed in the address bar.
   - If MapLibre succeeds while the manual request fails, the missing header is the difference.

## Typical fixes based on the diagnosis

| Diagnosis | Fix |
|-----------|-----|
| **Tile doesn’t exist at that zoom** | Adjust `minzoom`/`maxzoom` in the source definition, or generate tiles for the missing zoom levels. |
| **Missing `Accept` header** | Ensure the server is configured to serve vector tiles without requiring the header, or always request with `Accept: application/x-protobuf`. Most public services already do this, but self‑hosted Martin/TileServer‑GL may need `tilejson` `scheme: "xyz"` and proper MIME type. |
| **Range request required** | Use a server that supports plain GET (e.g., enable `range` handling in Martin) or register the `pmtiles://` protocol via `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', ...)` as described in the **maplibre‑pmtiles‑patterns** skill. |
| **Auth token missing** | Append the token to the URL (`?access_token=…`) or set the `Authorization` header via a custom `fetch` wrapper (MapLibre allows you to override `transformRequest`). |
| **Server bug / corrupted tiles** | Re‑generate the tiles (tippecanoe, planetiler, etc.) or fix the server configuration (e.g., correct `tileSize`, `encoding`, MIME type). |
| **CORS missing** (not a 500, but often confused) | Add `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` (or your domain) on the tile server. |

---

## Quick checklist you can run right now

1. **Do you have a TileJSON URL?**  
   - If yes, change the source to `"url": "https://tiles.example.com/tiles.json"` and drop the manual `tiles` array.

2. **Is the tile you’re testing at a zoom inside the advertised range?**  
   - Look at `minzoom` / `maxzoom` in the TileJSON (or the docs). Test a tile at `z = minzoom`.

3. **Add the proper Accept header** (use `curl` or the browser console):
   ```js
   fetch('https://tiles.example.com/14/8623/5678.pbf', {
     headers: { 'Accept': 'application/x-protobuf' }
   })
   .then(r => console.log(r.status));
   ```

4. **Check the Network tab for the exact request MapLibre makes** – copy the request URL and headers, then repeat them manually.

5. **If you control the server, look at its error log** for the 500 entry that matches the timestamp of your request.

---

### TL;DR

- **500 = server‑side error** – the request you typed is not being handled correctly.
- It can be caused by a missing tile, missing request headers, auth, or a genuine server bug.
- The fastest way to know which is which is to **inspect the request MapLibre actually sends** (Network tab) and compare it to the manual request, adding the `Accept: application/x-protobuf` header (and `Range` if needed).

Description: anti-pattern — a glyph URL is not a vector tile source (the .pbf collision)
prompt: My style's glyphs property points to https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf. Since it's already working and ends in .pbf, can I also register that same URL as a vector tile source, or do I need a separate one for tiles?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
No – the URL you give to the `glyphs` property is **only** for font‑glyph PBFs. It cannot be used as a vector‑tile source. You need a **different** URL (or TileJSON endpoint) that actually serves map data tiles.

---

## Why the two URLs are not interchangeable

| Aspect | Glyphs URL (`glyphs`) | Vector‑tile source (`url` / `tiles`) |
|--------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------|
| **What it returns** | Tiny PBF files that contain *font‑glyph* outlines for a single font‑stack and a single Unicode range (e.g. `0-255`, `256-511`, …). | PBF files that contain *geometric features* (points, lines, polygons) and their properties for a given **z/x/y** tile. |
| **Spec‑level type** | `glyphs` is a **style‑root property** (string template). | `type: "vector"` (or `"raster"`, `"raster-dem"`, …) is a **source definition**. |
| **Required metadata** | No TileJSON, no `vector_layers`. The URL template is the only thing the renderer needs. | Needs a TileJSON document (or a hand‑written `tiles` array) that tells MapLibre the tile URL template, zoom range, bounds, and (for vectors) the list of `source-layer` names. |
| **How MapLibre uses it** | When a `symbol` layer asks for a glyph (`text-font`), MapLibre builds a request like `https://example.com/fonts/Open+Sans%20Regular/0.pbf`. | When a vector layer asks for data, MapLibre builds a request like `https://example.com/tiles/12/3456/7890.pbf`. |
| **Typical MIME type** | `application/x-protobuf` (glyph PBF, ~few KB). | `application/x-protobuf` (vector tile PBF, often hundreds of KB) **or** an image format for raster sources. |

Because the two kinds of PBFs have completely different schemas, MapLibre will try to parse a glyph PBF as a vector tile (or vice‑versa) and will fail silently or throw a parsing error. The style spec does not allow a glyph URL to be referenced as a source.

---

## What you actually need for a vector‑tile source

1. **TileJSON endpoint (preferred)**  
   ```json
   {
     "type": "vector",
     "url": "https://example.com/tileset.json"
   }
   ```
   The JSON at `tileset.json` must contain at least:
   * `tiles`: an array of URL templates (`{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` etc.)
   * `minzoom` / `maxzoom` (optional but recommended)
   * `vector_layers`: an array describing each `source-layer` name and its fields (helps you pick the right `source-layer` in your style).

2. **Or a hand‑wired `tiles` array** (only if you have no TileJSON):
   ```json
   {
     "type": "vector",
     "tiles": ["https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"],
     "minzoom": 0,
     "maxzoom": 14
   }
   ```
   *Remember*: when you hand‑wire `tiles`, you must also supply `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. Otherwise MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22` and will request zoom levels that don’t exist, which often looks like “tiles disappear as you zoom in”.  

3. **CORS** – The tile server must send `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin:*` (or your domain) otherwise the browser will block the requests and you’ll see a blank map.

4. **`source-layer` matching** – After the source is added, every vector style layer that draws from it must specify the exact `source-layer` name that appears in the TileJSON’s `vector_layers`. A typo or a wrong name results in a silent “nothing draws” situation.

---

## Example: Adding both to the same map

```js
// 1️⃣ Glyphs – stays in the style JSON (or you can set it programmatically)
map.setStyle({
  version: 8,
  sources: { /* … */ },
  glyphs: "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  sprite: "https://example.com/sprites/basic",
  layers: [ /* … */ ]
});

// 2️⃣ Vector‑tile source – separate entry in the `sources` object
map.addSource('my-basemap', {
  type: 'vector',
  url: 'https://example.com/basemap/tiles.json'   // <-- NOT the glyphs URL
});

// 3️⃣ Use it in a layer
map.addLayer({
  id: 'roads',
  type: 'line',
  source: 'my-basemap',
  'source-layer': 'transportation',   // must match TileJSON schema
  paint: { 'line-color': '#777', 'line-width': 2 }
});
```

If you happen to host both the glyphs and the vector tiles under the same domain (e.g. `https://example.com/`), that’s fine, but the **paths** must be distinct (`/fonts/…` vs `/tiles/…`). The style spec will automatically request the correct asset type based on the context (glyph vs tile).

---

## Common pitfalls that look like “can I reuse the glyph URL?”

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Map shows no data, network tab shows 200 OK for the glyph URL but 404 for tile requests | You tried to add the glyph URL as a source. | Use a proper TileJSON or `tiles` array that points to real vector tiles. |
| Labels appear but are garbled or missing characters | Glyph URL is wrong or CORS‑blocked. | Verify the glyph endpoint returns valid glyph PBFs and that CORS headers are present. |
| `setFeatureState` never fires, but the layer draws | Vector source added, but `source-layer` is wrong → layer never receives features. | Check `vector_layers` in the TileJSON and match the `source-layer` exactly. |
| Tiles appear at the wrong zoom (e.g., everything looks “zoomed out”) | Raster source with default `tileSize: 512` but tiles are 256 px. | Add `tileSize: 256` to the raster source definition. (Not relevant for glyphs.) |

---

## TL;DR Checklist

- **Glyphs URL** → only for `glyphs` property. Do **not** register it as a source.
- **Vector tiles** → need a separate URL (TileJSON or `tiles` array) that serves map data.
- Keep both URLs under the same domain if you like, but they must point to **different endpoints** (`/fonts/…` vs `/tiles/…`).
- Verify CORS on both endpoints.
- When adding a vector source, always check the TileJSON’s `vector_layers` and use the exact `source-layer` names in your style layers.
- If you’re hand‑wiring `tiles`, remember to set `minzoom`/`maxzoom` (otherwise you’ll get “tiles disappear when you zoom”).  

That’s it – the glyph endpoint is a **font‑service**, not a map‑data service. Register a proper vector‑tile source separately, and your style will be able to draw both the basemap (or any vector data) **and** the labels/icons that rely on the glyphs you already have. Happy mapping!

Description: implicit — GeoParquet has no native MapLibre source, needs conversion
prompt: I have my dataset as GeoParquet (a .parquet file). Can I point a MapLibre GeoJSON source's `data` field directly at it, or reference it as a vector tile source?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
No – MapLibre GL JS cannot read a `.parquet` (GeoParquet) file directly, neither as a `geojson` source nor as a vector‑tile source. The browser only understands GeoJSON (or a JavaScript object) for a `geojson` source, and it only understands Mapbox Vector Tile (MVT) / PMTiles for a `vector` source.  

You have to **convert** the Parquet data to one of those formats (or serve it through a server that does the conversion on‑the‑fly).

Below is a quick‑reference guide that walks you through the options, the tools you can use, and the pitfalls to avoid.

---

## 1. Why Parquet doesn’t work out‑of‑the‑box

| Feature | What MapLibre expects | What a Parquet file is |
|---------|----------------------|------------------------|
| **GeoJSON source** (`type: "geojson"`) | A URL that returns a **JSON** document shaped like a GeoJSON FeatureCollection, or a JavaScript object passed directly to `data`. | A **binary column‑arithmetic** file (Apache Arrow/Parquet). The browser cannot parse it, and MapLibre has no built‑in decoder. |
| **Vector‑tile source** (`type: "vector"` or `"raster-dem"`) | A TileJSON endpoint (`url`) **or** a `tiles` array that points to **MVT (`.pbf`)** or **PMTiles** files. | Parquet does not contain pre‑rendered tiles; it is a *feature* store, not a *tile* store. |

Because of that, the only ways to get the data onto the map are:

1. **Convert the whole file to GeoJSON** and use a `geojson` source.  
2. **Generate vector tiles (MVT/PMTiles) from the Parquet data** and use a `vector` source.  
3. **Run a server that reads Parquet and streams GeoJSON or MVT on demand** (e.g. a custom API, `pg_tileserv` after loading into PostGIS, or a lightweight Node/Go service).

---

## 2. Converting GeoParquet → GeoJSON (for a `geojson` source)

### 2.1 One‑off conversion (static file)

```bash
# Using GDAL/ogr2ogr (works for most Parquet files)
ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON output.geojson input.parquet

# Using Python + geopandas (good for large files, you can filter)
python - <<'PY'
import geopandas as gpd
gdf = gpd.read_parquet('input.parquet')
gdf.to_file('output.geojson', driver='GeoJSON')
PY
```

*Tip:* If the dataset is huge (tens of MB+), consider **splitting** it into several smaller GeoJSON files or using a streaming approach (see 2.2).

### 2.2 On‑the‑fly conversion (dynamic endpoint)

If you don’t want to ship a massive static GeoJSON, expose a tiny HTTP endpoint that:

1. Reads the Parquet file (e.g. with `pyarrow`, `geopandas`, or `fastparquet`).  
2. Serialises the requested features to GeoJSON on each request.  

A minimal Flask example:

```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request
import geopandas as gpd

app = Flask(__name__)
gdf = gpd.read_parquet('data.parquet')   # load once at startup

@app.route('/tiles.geojson')
def serve_geojson():
    # optional: filter by bbox passed as ?bbox=minx,miny,maxx,maxy
    bbox = request.args.get('bbox')
    if bbox:
        minx, miny, maxx, maxy = map(float, bbox.split(','))
        subset = gdf.cx[minx:maxx, miny:maxy]
    else:
        subset = gdf
    return jsonify(subset.__geo_interface__)   # GeoJSON FeatureCollection
```

Then in MapLibre:

```js
map.addSource('my-data', {
  type: 'geojson',
  data: 'https://myserver.example.com/tiles.geojson'
});
```

*Remember:* The endpoint must send **CORS** headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your domain) or the browser will block the request.

---

## 3. Converting GeoParquet → Vector Tiles (MVT/PMTiles)

Vector tiles are the preferred way for anything larger than a few thousand features because they:

* Load only the tiles that intersect the current viewport.  
* Carry a built‑in zoom‑level hierarchy.  
* Work natively with `source-layer` filtering, `feature-state`, and high‑performance rendering.

### 3.1 Typical workflow

| Step | Tool | What it does |
|------|------|--------------|
| **Read Parquet → GeoJSON** | `geopandas`, `ogr2ogr`, `pyarrow` | Turns columnar data into a FeatureCollection (in memory). |
| **Tile‑generation** | `tippecanoe`, `tilemaker`, `martin`, `pmtiles` CLI | Consumes the GeoJSON and writes an **MBTiles** (SQLite) or **PMTiles** file containing MVT tiles. |
| **Serve** | `tileserver-gl`, `martin`, `pmtiles` (client‑side) | Exposes a TileJSON endpoint (`/tiles.json`) or a `pmtiles://` URL that MapLibre can consume. |

#### Example with Tippecanoe

```bash
# 1️⃣ Convert Parquet → GeoJSON (single file)
ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON data.geojson data.parquet

# 2️⃣ Generate MBTiles (MVT) – adjust --minimum-zoom / --maximum-zoom as needed
tippecanoe \
  --output=data.mbtiles \
  --minimum-zoom=0 \
  --maximum-zoom=14 \
  --layer=my_layer \
  --drop-densest-as-needed \
  data.geojson
```

#### Serve the MBTiles

*Option A – tileserver‑gl (Node.js)*

```bash
npx tileserver-gl data.mbtiles
# It will automatically expose a TileJSON at http://localhost:8080/data.json
```

*Option B – Martin (Rust, fast, works with PMTiles too)*

```bash
martin serve data.mbtiles --port 8080
# TileJSON: http://localhost:8080/data.json
```

*Option C – PMTiles (client‑side, no server)*

```bash
# Convert MBTiles → PMTiles (optional)
pmtiles convert data.mbtiles data.pmtiles

# Register the protocol in the browser (once, before map init)
import { register } from 'pmtiles';
register(new PMTiles('https://mycdn.example.com/data.pmtiles'));

# Then use the URL in the style:
{
  "id": "my-data",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://data.pmtiles"
}
```

### 3.2 What you need to watch for

| Issue | Why it matters | Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----|
| **Missing `source-layer`** | Vector sources require you to specify the exact layer name that exists inside the MVT tiles. | When you run `tippecanoe` you set `--layer=my_layer`. That string becomes the `source-layer`. Use that exact name in your style. |
| **Zoom range mismatch** | If you omit `minzoom`/`maxzoom` in the source definition, MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22`. Requests for zoom levels that don’t exist return empty tiles, giving the impression of a “blank map” at higher zooms. | Either let `tippecanoe` write the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom` into the TileJSON (default) **or** explicitly set them in the source definition. |
| **CORS** | Tile requests are cross‑origin. If the server (or CDN) doesn’t send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, the tiles are blocked and you see a blank map with no errors. | Configure your static host or tile server to send the header, or serve from the same origin. |
| **Tile size** | Raster sources default to 512 px tiles; vector tiles are always 512 px. No issue for MVT, but if you accidentally use a raster source for a 256 px tile service you’ll get a zoom‑offset. | Not relevant for MVT, but keep in mind if you ever add a raster basemap. |
| **Feature‑state IDs** | If you need `setFeatureState`, the vector tiles must contain a stable `id` field. Tippecanoe can promote a property to an ID with `--id-property=your_id`. | Add `--id-property=parcel_id` (or similar) when generating tiles, or use `promoteId` in the source definition. |

## 4. “Can I reference it as a vector tile source directly?” – The short answer is **no**, unless you first turn the Parquet data into a TileJSON‑compatible vector‑tile package (MVT/PMTiles).  

MapLibre’s `vector` source **does not read Parquet**; it only knows how to fetch:

* A TileJSON document (`url`) that lists `tiles: ["…/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"]` (MVT) **or** a `pmtiles://` URL.  
* Or a raw `tiles` array that points to those same `.pbf` files.

So the workflow is always **Parquet → (GeoJSON) → (MVT/PMTiles) → TileJSON → MapLibre**.

## 5. Quick checklist for getting your Parquet data on the map

| Step | Command / Code | Result |
|------|----------------|--------|
| **1. Convert** | `ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON data.geojson data.parquet` | `data.geojson` (or stream via API) |
| **2. Tile‑gen** | `tippecanoe --output=data.mbtiles --layer=my_layer data.geojson` | `data.mbtiles` containing MVT tiles |
| **3. Serve** | `martin serve data.mbtiles --port 8080` | TileJSON at `http://localhost:8080/data.json` |
| **4. Add source** | ```js\nmap.addSource('my-data', { type: 'vector', url: 'http://localhost:8080/data.json' });\n``` | Source ready |
| **5. Add layer** | ```json\n{ \"id\": \"my-fill\", \"type\": \"fill\", \"source\": \"my-data\", \"source-layer\": \"my_layer\", \"paint\": { \"fill-color\": \"#ff6600\", \"fill-opacity\": 0.5 } }\n``` | Data appears on the map |
| **6. (Optional) Feature state** | Add `promoteId: 'parcel_id'` to the source if you need IDs. | `setFeatureState` works. |
